title: Samantabhadra's promise (Kern ch. 26)
hook: the bodhisattva of practice promises to protect those who keep the sutra

segments.voice: Yesterday, two princes walked on the air until their father asked who had taught them. Your line: the sons led the king.

The Lotus Sutra is nearly over when, in chapter twenty-six, a late guest arrives from a world far to the east, with a great company behind him. His name is Samantabhadra. He bows and asks the Buddha a practical question, the kind someone asks near the end of a long meeting. After you are gone, how will people get hold of this teaching? What does it take?
screen: `A LATE GUEST FROM THE EAST.` → `HIS NAME IS SAMANTABHADRA.` → `HOW WILL PEOPLE KEEP THIS?`

segments.voice: The Buddha answers with a short list. Roughly: be held in the care of the Buddhas, plant roots of goodness, join the company of those set on the path, and turn the mind toward freeing all beings. Then Samantabhadra makes his promise, and it's surprisingly concrete. Whoever keeps this sutra, he says, I will guard. When they walk and turn the teaching over in their mind, I'll come riding a white elephant with six tusks and stand before them. When they sit and reflect on it, I'll come again. And if they forget a line, even one word, I'll be there to give it back. He adds protective spells, so nothing harmful can find an opening, and the Buddha praises him. Look at what the promise is attached to. Not to being clever, not to being finished. To keeping: reading, remembering, turning the words over while walking. The protection follows the practice, step for step. In the traditions that honor him, Samantabhadra is the bodhisattva of practice, of vows actually carried out. It's the week's last day, so look back at the end of the Lotus. Spells to guard those who keep it. The Medicine King's offering. Gadgadasvara in many forms. Guanyin hearing every cry, in a chapter chanted on its own. Two sons leading a king. And now a bodhisattva on a white elephant. Week after week the Lotus has said: this is precious. This week it added: you won't be left alone with it.
screen: `HOW TO GET HOLD OF THE TEACHING.` · `A WHITE ELEPHANT WITH SIX TUSKS.` · `A FORGOTTEN LINE, GIVEN BACK.` · `THE PROTECTION FOLLOWS THE PRACTICE.` · then, large: `KEPT AND PROTECTED.`

segments.voice: Choose one small practice you already keep, or would like to: this sit, a line you say in the morning, a walk without your phone, watering a plant. Make it small enough to do tomorrow on a bad day. Hold it the way you'd hold a promise to a friend, just for tomorrow, not forever.
Samantabhadra's promise. To come, on a white elephant, to anyone who keeps the sutra, and to give back any line they forget. Today's word.
Your line: kept and protected. Even a forgotten line can be given back. That's the week, and nearly the whole Lotus.

howItsDone: In East Asian Mahayana traditions Samantabhadra is honored as the bodhisattva of practice and vows, and temple images show him seated on a white elephant; communities that keep the Lotus Sutra read this chapter as his pledge to protect them.

chat.who: a friend from your yoga class
chat.says: What does Samantabhadra promise near the end of the Lotus Sutra?
options: To come on a white elephant to whoever keeps the sutra, and give back lines they forget.
To make anyone who reads the sutra rich and healthy for the rest of their life.
To appear only to monks who have finished studying every chapter of the sutra.
chat.meaning: Samantabhadra promises to guard whoever keeps the sutra, coming when they walk or sit with it. The protection follows the practice, not being finished.

notes: Chapter paraphrased from Kern (1884) ch. 26, not quoted. Confirm the Buddha's short list of conditions (Kern: four qualities). 'Four' is left out of the voice on purpose.
'A white elephant with six tusks': confirm Kern's wording in ch. 26.
Promise to appear when the keeper walks and when they sit, and to restore forgotten words: confirm against Kern.
'Bodhisattva of practice' is the outline's description and an East Asian reception; confirm. howItsDone says temple images show him on a white elephant; confirm the phrasing.
